metaTitle: Types of Mice: House, Deer and White-Footed
metaDescription: Three types of mice turn up in US homes: house, deer and white-footed. Compare size, coat and tail, rule out look-alikes, and see which carry hantavirus.
h1: Types of Mice in the US: How to Tell Which One You Have
dek: A side-by-side guide to the house mouse, deer mouse and white-footed mouse, the voles, shrews and young rats that get called mice, which ones come indoors, and which carry hantavirus.
excerpt: House mouse, deer mouse or white-footed mouse? Compare size, coat and tail, rule out voles, shrews and young rats, and see which mice carry hantavirus.

quickAnswer.lead: **Three kinds of mice commonly live in or enter US homes: the house mouse, the deer mouse and the white-footed mouse.** The house mouse is gray-brown all over with a nearly hairless tail; the other two are brown above with white bellies and feet. [CDC identifies the deer mouse and the white-footed mouse as hantavirus hosts](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr5109a1.htm), so check the coat and tail before you clean up after any mouse.
bullets: A house mouse is 5 to 7 inches long including its 3- to 4-inch tail and weighs about 1/2 ounce, by the University of California's figures.
A deer mouse is 6 1/2 to 8 inches long with a 3- to 4-inch furred tail that is dark on top and white underneath.
A white-footed mouse is 6 to 7 1/2 inches long and looks much like a deer mouse, but its 2 1/2- to 3 1/2-inch tail is shorter for its body.
CDC's 2002 recommendations report that on average about 10 percent of deer mice tested show evidence of Sin Nombre virus infection, and infected mice do not look sick.
Deer mice and white-footed mice enter structures from fall through spring, while house mice can live their whole lives indoors.
Voles have short tails and almost never enter houses; shrews have pointed snouts and eat insects.

body.text: What types of mice live in and around US homes?

Three kinds of mice commonly live in or enter US homes: the house mouse (*Mus musculus*), the deer mouse (*Peromyscus maniculatus*) and the white-footed mouse (*Peromyscus leucopus*). [Cornell University's page on mouse and rat biology](https://cals.cornell.edu/integrated-pest-management/outreach-education/whats-bugging-you/rodents/mouse-and-rat-biology-and-behaviour) names those three, along with the Norway rat, as the common pest rodents in New York. [The Pennsylvania Game Commission's wildlife note on mice and voles](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/pgc/wildlife/discover-pa-wildlife/mice-and-voles) explains where they come from: it counts the deer mouse and the white-footed mouse as that state's two native mice, and it describes the house mouse as an Old World species brought to North America by European settlers.

The three look alike at a glance, but the species changes the health picture and the cleanup. CDC lists the deer mouse and the white-footed mouse as hosts of the hantaviruses that cause a severe lung illness, and the house mouse is not on that list. The table sets the three side by side, and the [complete guide to mice control](/learn/mice) covers what to do about any of them.

body.text: How do you identify a house mouse?

A house mouse is the plain one: light brownish to gray over the whole body, with a long tail that has almost no fur on it. [The University of California's Pest Notes on the house mouse](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/house-mouse/) put an adult at 5 to 7 inches long including the 3- to 4-inch tail and about 1/2 ounce, with relatively large ears and small black eyes.

Other sources measure it a little differently. Cornell gives the body alone as 2.5 to 3.75 inches and the tail as 2.75 to 4 inches, and the Pennsylvania note gives 6 to 8 inches overall with a 3-inch scaly tail. The ranges differ by an inch or so, but the description does not: UC IPM (the university's Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program) calls the coat gray overall, and Cornell calls it uniformly grayish brown.

body.needed: Side-view photo of an adult house mouse on a plain background beside an inch ruler, showing the uniform gray-brown coat with no white belly line, the large ears and the long, nearly hairless tail

body.text: This is the mouse built for indoor life. Cornell notes that house mice can live their entire lives inside a building, and UC IPM says they seldom venture more than 30 feet from their nest and food supply, so signs in one spot point to a nest nearby. UC IPM names the signs to look for: droppings, fresh gnaw marks and tracks, plus a musky odor in large or long-term infestations. A separate guide shows [what mouse droppings look like, fresh and old](/blog/what-does-mouse-poop-look-like-canada).

House mice also outbreed their native relatives. UC IPM credits a female with 5 to 10 litters a year of about 5 or 6 pups, while the Pennsylvania figures for deer mice and white-footed mice are three or four litters a year of three to seven young. On health, UC IPM lists leptospirosis, salmonella and lymphocytic choriomeningitis (LCM) among the diseases house mice carry and notes that their urine is a major source of allergens.
How do you tell a deer mouse from a house mouse?

Look at the tail and the belly. [UC IPM's deer mouse guide](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/deer-mouse/) calls the two-toned tail, dark on top and white underneath, the easiest feature for separating a deer mouse from a house mouse, whose tail is almost furless. The deer mouse also has white undersides, legs and feet, and UC's house mouse page describes a distinct line where the dark back meets the white belly. Its eyes and ears are typically larger than a house mouse's.

body.text: Size will not settle it. The Pennsylvania Game Commission gives the deer mouse 6 1/2 to 8 inches of total length, 3 to 4 inches of that being fur-covered tail, and a weight of 0.4 to 1 ounce, which overlaps its figures for the house mouse almost entirely, and Cornell describes both native mice as about the same size and shape as a house mouse. The shade of the back can mislead too. Adults are brownish gray above, but the same note says juveniles are gray for their first month, so go by the belly and the tail.

The deer mouse is a country mouse. UC IPM calls it the most abundant and widely distributed mammal in North America, and the Pennsylvania note gives its range as the Northeast, the Midwest and the West from Alaska to Mexico. [CDC's hantavirus risk-reduction recommendations](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr5109a1.htm), issued in 2002, describe it as common and widespread in rural areas through much of the United States. UC IPM adds that deer mice are not common in urban and residential areas unless large or numerous parks or fields are nearby.

Buildings are another matter. UC IPM says deer mice are small enough to get into many of them and often enter vacated homes, cabins and other structures, where they build nests and store food. The [deer mouse profile](/blog/deer-mice) goes deeper on the animal's habits and on keeping it out of cabins and sheds.
What is a white-footed mouse, and is it different from a deer mouse?

The white-footed mouse is a separate species in the same genus as the deer mouse, and it looks much like one except that its tail is shorter in relation to its body. That is how the Pennsylvania Game Commission separates the two: the white-footed mouse measures 6 to 7 1/2 inches overall with a 2 1/2- to 3 1/2-inch tail, against the deer mouse's 3- to 4-inch tail. The note describes the coat as reddish brown above with a white belly and feet, and the weight as 0.6 to 1 ounce.

The name causes confusion of its own. UC IPM notes that the deer mouse is itself often referred to as a white-footed mouse, that California alone has seven species of *Peromyscus*, and that they are difficult to distinguish from one another. The common name by itself does not tell you the species.

The white-footed mouse is no stranger to buildings. The Pennsylvania note lists farm buildings and houses among the places it lives, alongside woods, shrubby areas, fields and stream margins, and describes an agile climber that caches seeds in autumn. CDC singles out the deer mouse and the white-footed mouse as the only hantavirus hosts commonly associated with the areas around homes.

For a homeowner, the practical answer is that you do not need to split these two. Both are hantavirus hosts and both call for the same careful cleanup. Common names get looser still with field mouse, which the Pennsylvania note says is what the meadow vole is often called; a separate guide untangles [what people mean by field mice](/blog/field-mice).
Which types of mice carry hantavirus?

In the United States the deer mouse and the white-footed mouse do, and the house mouse is not among the known hosts. CDC's recommendations identify the deer mouse as the host of Sin Nombre virus, the primary cause of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in this country, and the white-footed mouse as the host of New York virus. Two rats complete the list: the cotton rat (Black Creek Canal virus) and the rice rat (Bayou virus). Nearly all of the continental United States lies within the range of at least one of these four.

The house mouse and the Norway and black rats sit outside that group. CDC states that every hantavirus known to cause HPS is carried by New World rats and mice, and it places those three familiar pests in a different subfamily. That does not make a house mouse harmless, as the disease list in the house mouse section shows. It means HPS is not the concern with that species.

You cannot pick out an infected mouse by looking. CDC reports that on average about 10 percent of deer mice tested across the species' range show evidence of Sin Nombre infection, though the share varies by place and time, and that hantaviruses do not cause obvious illness in the rodents that carry them. Infected rodents shed the virus in saliva, urine and droppings, and people are most often infected by inhaling it once it is airborne. For the general public, CDC's advice is to treat every wild mouse or rat met in a rural area as though it were infected. UC IPM puts the fatality rate of HPS at about 36 percent and says there is no evidence that North American hantaviruses spread from one person to another.

body.title: Before you clean up after any wild mouse
body.text: UC IPM's method: air the space out for at least 30 minutes, wear nonfabric gloves (rubber, latex, vinyl or nitrile), thoroughly wet droppings, nests and trapped mice with a disinfectant or a bleach solution (1 1/2 cups of household bleach in 1 gallon of water), let it soak for 10 minutes before wiping up with a damp towel, and never sweep or vacuum; use any disinfectant as its label directs. Contact a healthcare provider if you become ill after contact with rodents or their droppings, and mention the exposure.
The full sequence, including nests and dead mice, is in the guide to [removing mice and cleaning up after them](/blog/mice-removal).
Which animals get mistaken for mice?

Voles, shrews, young rats and jumping mice are the usual look-alikes, and each has a feature that gives it away. UC IPM's house mouse page sums up the first two in a line: voles have short tails, and shrews have pointed snouts and tiny eyes.

body.text: Voles

A vole is a stocky, short-tailed rodent of grassy ground, and it almost never enters houses. [Iowa State University Extension's page on vole damage](https://naturalresources.extension.iastate.edu/wildlife/problem/vole-tracks-grass) describes the meadow vole as chestnut brown, with longish fur that almost hides its small ears and eyes, short legs, and a tail that is usually no more than an inch long. The Pennsylvania Game Commission measures the same species at 6 to 7.6 inches overall with a 1.3- to 2.5-inch tail and a weight of 0.7 to 2.3 ounces. The two sources differ on the tail, but both call it short, and even the longer figure is under the 3 to 4 inches of a house mouse or deer mouse tail.

The signs differ too. Iowa State describes surface runways 1 to 2 inches across, with the vegetation clipped close or dead along the well-used ones, and bark gnawed from young trees and shrubs, mostly in fall and winter.
Shrews

A shrew is not a mouse at all. Iowa State describes it as an insect-eating mammal that is a close relative of the mole and no relation of the vole it can resemble. The pointed snout and tiny eyes that UC IPM mentions are the field marks. Shrews belong on this page for one reason: Iowa State notes that the short-tailed shrew does get into houses, so a small furry animal in the basement is not automatically a mouse.
Young rats

A young rat is told from a mouse by its ears, eyes and nose. Cornell's comparison is that a house mouse, set against a young or juvenile rat, has large ears and eyes and a pointier nose; read the other way, the young rat is the one with the less prominent ears and eyes and the blunter nose. Droppings help when you never see the animal: Cornell gives mouse droppings as 1/8 to 1/4 inch long, roof rat droppings as about 1/2 inch and Norway rat droppings as 3/4 to 1 inch. An adult Norway rat is no look-alike: Cornell says it can reach a total length of 16 inches with its tail. A separate guide shows [how baby mice differ from baby rats](/blog/baby-mice).
Jumping mice

Jumping mice are long-tailed wild mice of fields and forest. The Pennsylvania note describes the meadow jumping mouse as 8 to 9 inches long, 5 to 6 inches of it tail, yellowish brown with a dark stripe down the back, orangish sides and a white belly and feet. It lives in moist grassy and brushy fields and along woodland edges, usually moves in short hops of a foot or two, and hibernates underground from October or November until late April or early May. The woodland jumping mouse, a forest relative with a white-tipped tail, can leap up to ten feet.
Which types of mice come indoors, and when?
House mice can be indoors in any month, and the two native mice come in mainly from fall through spring, according to Cornell. The other animals on this page are mostly outdoor finds:

items: **House mouse.** Year-round; Cornell notes it can live its entire life inside a structure.

**Deer mouse and white-footed mouse.** Fall through spring. UC IPM adds that deer mice often enter vacated homes, cabins and other structures, and that they are uncommon in urban neighborhoods without large parks or fields nearby.
**Voles.** Almost never, according to Iowa State.
**Shrews.** Sometimes; the short-tailed shrew does get into houses.
**Jumping mice.** The sources used here do not report them indoors, and they hibernate underground through the cold months.

body.text: That calendar is the argument for closing up a house before fall. UC IPM calls rodent-proof construction the most effective and permanent way to keep deer mice out of buildings. Start with the guide to [sealing a house against mice before winter](/blog/how-to-keep-mice-out-of-your-house-winter), and for the gaps themselves see [how to use steel wool as a mouse barrier](/blog/steel-wool-for-mice).
Does the type of mouse change what you should do?

It changes the cleanup more than the overall plan. Whatever the species, the work is the same three jobs: close the entry points, trap the animals already inside, and clean up safely. The differences are these:

items: **House mouse.** Expect a resident, breeding population close to the food. Because house mice seldom range more than 30 feet from the nest, look for the signs first; the guide to [mouse traps and where to set them](/blog/mice-traps) covers placement.
**Deer mouse or white-footed mouse.** Trap the same way, but treat every dropping, nest and dead mouse as a possible hantavirus source and use the wet-cleaning method described above.
**Not sure which.** Use the hantavirus precautions anyway. CDC's recommendation for the general public covers all wild mice and rats in rural areas, not only the ones you can name.
**Young rat.** Confirm with the droppings, then switch to [methods meant for rats](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-rats-canada).
**Vole or shrew.** Indoor mouse control is the wrong tool. Voles do their damage outdoors, to grass and to the bark of young trees and shrubs, and shrews eat insects.

body.text: If you cannot identify the animal, or the droppings are widespread, that is a reasonable point to bring in a professional. Ask whoever you hire to name the species they find. The guide to [hiring a mice exterminator](/blog/mice-exterminator) lists the other questions worth asking and what the job includes.

faqs.question: Which type of mouse lives in houses all year?
faqs.answer: The house mouse. Cornell's rodent biology page says house mice can live their entire lives indoors, and the University of California describes them as living near people in and around homes, schools and commercial settings, seldom venturing more than 30 feet from the nest and food supply. Deer mice and white-footed mice behave differently: Cornell says they enter structures from fall through spring, and the University of California notes that deer mice often move into vacated homes and cabins.

faqs.question: Do house mice carry hantavirus?
faqs.answer: House mice are not among the known hosts of the hantaviruses that cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome. CDC states that all hantaviruses known to cause that illness are carried by New World rats and mice, a group that includes the deer mouse and white-footed mouse but not the house mouse or the Norway and black rats. House mice are still a health concern. The University of California lists leptospirosis, salmonella and lymphocytic choriomeningitis among the diseases they carry and says their urine is a major source of allergens. Contact a healthcare provider if you become ill after contact with any rodent.

faqs.question: Is a white-footed mouse the same as a deer mouse?
faqs.answer: No. They are two species in the same genus, Peromyscus. The Pennsylvania Game Commission says the white-footed mouse looks much like a deer mouse except that its tail is shorter in relation to its body: 2 1/2 to 3 1/2 inches on a mouse 6 to 7 1/2 inches long, against 3 to 4 inches on a deer mouse of 6 1/2 to 8 inches. For a homeowner the difference rarely matters, because CDC lists both as hantavirus hosts and the same cleanup precautions apply to each.

faqs.question: Do all deer mice carry hantavirus?
faqs.answer: No. CDC's 2002 risk-reduction recommendations report that on average about 10 percent of deer mice tested across the species' range show evidence of infection with Sin Nombre virus, a share that varies by place and time. The difficulty is that hantaviruses do not cause obvious illness in the rodents that carry them, so an infected mouse looks like any other. That is why CDC recommends that the public treat every wild mouse or rat met in a rural area as though it were infected, and why droppings and nests should be wetted with disinfectant and never swept or vacuumed.

faqs.question: How can I tell a mouse from a baby rat?
faqs.answer: Compare the features of the head. Cornell's rodent biology page says that, compared with a juvenile rat, a house mouse has large ears and eyes and a pointier nose, so the young rat is the one whose ears and eyes look less prominent and whose nose looks blunter. Droppings are a second check: Cornell gives mouse droppings as 1/8 to 1/4 inch long, roof rat droppings as about 1/2 inch and Norway rat droppings as 3/4 to 1 inch. A full-grown Norway rat is far larger than any mouse: Cornell says it can reach a total length of 16 inches including the tail.

faqs.question: Are voles a type of mouse, and do they come in the house?
faqs.answer: Voles are rodents that resemble mice, but they are not the mice that infest homes. Iowa State University Extension says voles almost never enter houses. You can recognize one by its stocky body, small ears nearly hidden in fur and short tail, which Iowa State puts at usually no more than an inch and the Pennsylvania Game Commission at 1.3 to 2.5 inches for the meadow vole. Their sign is outdoors: runways 1 to 2 inches wide through grass and gnawed bark on young trees and shrubs, mostly in fall and winter.
